episodes.title: People are doing $100M+ in sales on this app
recap: **Shaan bought a crab on the internet, and that's the whole thesis.** The episode opens with Shaan confessing he bought a $34 crab pack from a fisherman live-streaming on Whatnot — a seller called "I Love Crabs" with 3,300 sales and north of $100K made. It's a funny bit, but it's also the pitch for the company: live auctions turn wildly niche products into entertainment, and entertainment sells. Whatnot started with Funko Pops and Pokémon cards and now moves everything from gold bars to fresh seafood, on the way to a roughly $20 billion valuation in about six and a half years.

**The idea came from an eBay data scrape, not a vision.** Grant and co-founder Logan first tried to build a "better full-service Craigslist" — until two calls with delivery execs (one ran logistics for Bob's Discount Furniture) proved the per-delivery cost would eat any margin on used goods. So Grant went hunting for broken marketplaces and kept landing on eBay. Using a tool that exposed category-level sales, they plotted every collectibles category over time and saw them all ripping — with more Funkos sold on eBay than comic books. Add a gut sense that a nostalgia-driven, 30-something buyer wanted something more social than a 20-year-old listing page, and you have the pivot.

**Solve the chicken-and-egg by being the egg.** With no sellers and no buyers, Whatnot made itself the only seller. It listed Funkos it didn't own, priced them with a homemade algorithm (past 10 sales plus a liquidity floor, so it never listed anything it couldn't actually source), authenticated them as a value-add, and had a small team in Brazil hunt down stock from about 100 online stores once someone ordered. Early pricing bugs meant collectors happily bought $500 Funkos for $150. Only when demand was real — around late February 2020 — did they open the doors to outside sellers, and even then they cross-listed sellers' inventory onto other marketplaces under Whatnot's account so new sellers got sales fast enough to stick around.

**The growth hack was a raffle with unlimited shares.** Whatnot gave away a "grail" Funko worth $500–$1,000 every week, and every referral, code use, Twitter share or Instagram share earned another entry. The first one flopped: 104 entries, maybe 30–40 accounts, zero purchases, all paid for out of Grant's savings. But the second drew around 250, about 2.5x — enough of a compounding signal to keep going, and soon they'd effectively taken over the Funko subreddits and Facebook groups. Grant's rule: early on you can't win the obvious channels (they spent almost nothing on paid ads then, "an obscene amount" now), so find an unfair edge nobody else can copy.

**The numbers look like a hockey stick drawn by a toddler.** December 2019: about 30 sales, several of them mispricings. Launch of live auctions in July 2020 sent growth to 100%+ month over month; 2020 closed at $2.3M in sales with 17–18 people. 2021: about $163M with roughly 100 employees. 2022: a billion in sales — and a billion-dollar valuation only about 20 months after those 30 sales. Grant credits the live format (transformational for sellers, many of whom closed their brick-and-mortar shops), a lights-out first 30 hires, and a repeatable playbook for launching new categories that cross-pollinate.

**"Stories are sort of BS."** Grant's recurring theme is distrust of tidy narratives. Investors balked at a "small" Funko market, but almost every giant started in a niche; eBay's real first sale was a broken laser pointer to a broken-laser-pointer collector (the PEZ story was PR). His other contrarian takes: don't hire fancy executives just because of their logos, and don't bet on being a "vision-driven" company. Whatnot calls itself user-driven: have a direction, but if customers don't want it, you're dead.

**Explain it like I'm in middle school.** As CEO of 1,400 people, Grant's superpower is going all the way to the bottom of a problem. His example: the discovery team swore an A/B test proved a feed change was fine, but A/B tests break on two-sided networks because shifting buyers changes how sellers behave on both sides of the test. Plotting seller "elasticity curves" — how much a seller's business grows or shrinks as you add or remove impressions — showed some sellers lost far more than engagement gained. He insists people drop the jargon, and if you can't explain it simply, you probably don't know it. Shaan compares it to Emmett Shear's Socratic grillings at Twitch.

**Disagreeable without being a jerk, and fast without saying so.** Grant left Facebook after a senior leader torched a team in a product review he'd sweated over for weeks; he learned that being mean almost never gets better work. So he's softened his early "this sucks" Slack style for a company where people mostly know him from Zoom. On speed: "If you think you're moving fast, you're probably not" — if you have time to talk about it, you're too slow.

**Live commerce is a 20–30x opportunity, and picks-and-shovels are wide open.** Grant thinks live shopping will be 30%+ of e-commerce within a decade (it's ~40% in China; single digits in the US/Europe today). Whatnot's biggest sellers already do well into nine figures — one started as three or four people and now employs 150–200 almost entirely on Whatnot. The adjacent plays he names: wholesale marketplaces supplying sellers with inventory, and "MCNs" (multi-channel networks) that help sellers run their live businesses.
fun_facts: Grant sold Pokémon cards on Yahoo Auctions and eBay as a kid, and a holographic Chansey bought for $10 by money order 20 years ago made a cameo on the show ("our paths crossed").
Whatnot's first engineer was a brilliant-but-difficult former colleague in Brazil; the designer worked purely for equity.
Shaan's diary notes from first meeting Grant: "Looks like a soccer dad… quiet intensity, humble confidence… winner energy. We should invest." He didn't follow up, and missed the round.
The founders bought about 50 random domains (including SEO plays like "used Peloton") while drinking in a Tokyo bar.
Popular items this year: NeeDoh squishy toys, gold and silver bars sold direct by mints, and live crab.
Grant collects "type one" photographs (original prints) and still plays hockey. He's Canadian.
discussion_questions: Whatnot only opened to outside sellers once its own fake-inventory storefront had proven buyer demand. Which marketplace ideas today could you launch the same way, as the only seller, and what would your "liquidity floor" be?
Grant says A/B tests mislead on two-sided networks because both sides react. Where else might a confident "we tested it" be hiding a second-order effect in your own product or business?

highlights.text: Whatnot found its market by scraping eBay's category-level sales: every collectibles category was growing, and more Funkos sold than comic books.
Solve the marketplace chicken-and-egg by being the only seller. Whatnot listed Funkos it didn't own, priced from the last 10 sales plus a liquidity floor, and sourced each one after it sold.
New sellers churn if they don't sell fast, so Whatnot cross-listed their inventory on other marketplaces under its own account to get them early sales.
A weekly grail raffle where every referral or share earned an entry: the first drew 104 entries and no sales, the second about 250. A 2.5x signal was enough to keep going.
From about 30 sales in December 2019 to $2.3M in 2020, $163M in 2021 and a billion in 2022, driven by live auctions growing 100%+ month over month.
A/B tests break on two-sided networks because both sides react. Plot seller elasticity curves to see who loses when you shift impressions.
Grant's tests for depth and speed: if you can't explain it like you're in middle school you don't know it, and if you have time to talk about moving fast, you're too slow.
Live shopping is about 40% of e-commerce in China and single digits in the US. The open plays are wholesale marketplaces for sellers and networks that run sellers' live businesses.

episodes.title: Stand-Up Comedy Pt I
recap: **Stand-up was born in vaudeville's gaps.** Being funny in front of a crowd is as old as speech, but the modern form grew out of vaudeville emcees telling jokes between acts. Charlie Case, the son of a freeborn Black man and an Irish mother, is often named as the first: he joined vaudeville around 1880, got fed up with being forced into blackface, and by about 1900 was doing something that looks like a stand-up act — billed as "the man who talks about his father." Josh and Chuck note that talking about your parents has been roughly 90% of stand-up ever since.

**The Borscht Belt wrote the rulebook.** From the 1930s, Jewish resorts in the Catskills and Adirondacks became summer residencies where comics bounced from hotel to hotel, often starting out as social directors. That's where the joke-dense, self-deprecating style took shape: Henny Youngman ("take my wife, please") could fire off about 50 jokes in eight minutes. The circuit lasted into the 1970s and launched Mel Brooks, Sid Caesar, Jackie Mason, and even a young Jerry Seinfeld. Its Black counterpart was the Chitlin' Circuit, home to Redd Foxx, Flip Wilson and Moms Mabley.

**The 1950s "sick comedians" made it personal.** In San Francisco clubs like the hungry i, Mort Sahl sat on stage with a newspaper and went after whoever held power, which he says got him blacklisted by Kennedy liberals. Shelley Berman had the first gold comedy record and the first non-music Grammy, and Jonathan Winters joked about his time in mental hospitals. Lenny Bruce got arrested repeatedly on obscenity charges and became a free-speech landmark (the hosts disagree on how funny he was). Time magazine lumped them together as "sick comedians" in 1959: comedy built on point of view rather than recycled jokes.

**The counterculture trinity of Carlin, Pryor and Klein.** George Carlin started out in a suit telling clean jokes, then reinvented himself in the early '70s with the "seven words you can't say on television." Richard Pryor is described as the first Black comedian who didn't code-switch for white audiences. Robert Klein, a Borscht Belt alum, mixed social commentary with pure personality. Josh pushes back that Klein feels more observational than countercultural.

**The real engine was distribution.** Comedy clubs like the Improv (which grew to 15 locations) and the Comedy Store (Mitzi Shore took it over in 1972 in a divorce settlement) gave comics places to workshop several nights a week. Then came the amplifiers: Carson's couch as the industry's seal of approval, LPs that made comedy records Grammy material, HBO specials starting with Robert Klein in 1975, Rodney Dangerfield's Young Comedians specials, Def Comedy Jam, and early Comedy Central, which was pretty much nothing but stand-up clips. Each new channel changed what you could say and how many people heard it.

**Superstars, and the ones who walked away.** Steve Martin was the first comic to sell out arenas, until 20,000 people chanting his punchlines back at him drained the fun and he quit stand-up for movies. Robin Williams was so naturally manic that cocaine apparently calmed him down. Joan Rivers killed on late night so hard she nearly replaced Carson, then lost his favor by pursuing her own show without telling him. Eddie Murphy came out of SNL at 19 and later mentored Chris Rock.

**Then the comics became sitcoms.** Networks figured out that even stand-ups who can't act can play themselves. That gave us Seinfeld, Drew Carey, Jamie Foxx, Bernie Mac, Roseanne, Everybody Loves Raymond and Home Improvement, plus shorter-lived ones like Norm, Whitney and Mulaney. Seinfeld famously held up his Emmy and said, "I am a bad actor." Part II picks up with alt comedy in the '90s.
fun_facts: "Ginger did everything Fred did, only backwards and in heels" is often credited to Joan Rivers, according to the hosts' research.
Henny Youngman averaged under 10 seconds per joke.
Steve Martin once did a set for dogs on Carson, including a bit on a dog whistle humans can't hear.
Hugh Hefner discovered Dick Gregory in 1961 and gave him time at the Chicago Playboy Club.
Bob Hope, who brought stand-up from the resorts to the mainstream, was born in Britain and was one of the first to use a team of writers on current events.
discussion_questions: Each leap in stand-up (clubs, LPs, HBO, Comedy Central) followed a new distribution channel. What is today's version, whether podcasts, TikTok or Netflix specials, and how is it changing what jokes get written?
Mort Sahl said his blacklisting came from his own political side, not the other. Is "punch whoever's in charge" still a viable comedic stance when audiences are this polarized?

highlights.text: Charlie Case is often named the first stand-up: around 1900 he was billed as "the man who talks about his father," after refusing to keep performing in blackface.
The Borscht Belt resorts of the Catskills set stand-up's joke-dense, self-deprecating style. Henny Youngman could tell about 50 jokes in eight minutes.
Time magazine called the 1950s wave of Mort Sahl, Shelley Berman and Lenny Bruce "sick comedians": comedy built on a point of view rather than recycled jokes.
Stand-up's growth followed distribution: clubs to workshop in, Carson's couch, comedy LPs, HBO specials from 1975, then Comedy Central. Each channel changed what comics could say.
Mitzi Shore got the Comedy Store in a 1972 divorce settlement and turned it into one of the industry's key workshops.
Steve Martin was the first comic to sell out arenas, then quit stand-up when 20,000 people chanting his punchlines back took the fun out of it.
Networks learned that stand-ups who can't act can still play themselves, which produced Seinfeld, Roseanne, Home Improvement and Everybody Loves Raymond.

episodes.title: Did AI Write This?
recap: **Pangram is the receipt everyone waves around.** When a prize-winning novel, a seven-figure book deal or a newspaper op-ed gets accused of being AI-written, the screenshot people post is usually from Pangram. Max Spero's problem is building a tool that reliably tells whether text, and now images, came from a model. Its biggest markets are education (K-12 through higher ed) and publishing. Max frames the tool as adding friction to cheating rather than ending it: if you can't one-shot an assignment and have to rebuild it from "AI bones," fewer students bother.

**Publishing got blindsided because editors don't use chatbots.** Max's explanation for this year's run of book scandals is that editors and publishers spend their days reading real books, so they never developed an instinct for AI prose and were caught off guard when it became good enough to publish. Jacob brings up investor Stanley Druckenmiller, who replied to accusations about his Wall Street Journal op-ed with roughly "you're damn right AI wrote that, I'm 80 and I know how to use it," while the editor shrugged that ghostwriting is normal anyway. Max's line is that using AI to compress (turning five pages of your own research into op-ed length) is fine, but using it to pad (turning a few bullet points into an essay) is a disservice to readers. Jacob's version: "Just publish the bullet points, bro."

**Why all AI slop sounds the same.** Max points to mode collapse: once a model learns the most common word, phrase or sentence shape, it pushes out the edges of its distribution and keeps producing the middle. Post-training adds to it. If a reward model learned that em dashes and "it's not just X, it's Y" correlate with good writing before AI existed, the model turns those up to 11. The good news for Jacob is that em dashes stopped being a tell after the GPT-4o era, so he can use them again.

**The arms race: watermarks, humanizers, and the incentive problem.** Max says the frontier labs could build detectors but either don't prioritize it or have reasons not to. He cites reporting that OpenAI built text watermarking and shelved it, worried that students, a big part of its user base, would get caught or switch to another tool. The EU now requires watermarks on language model text, and Google already does it. Watermarks are encoded statistically in word choice, so retyping won't remove them, but a paraphraser will. "Humanizer" tools try to slip past detectors, so Pangram trains on their output; Jacob's own test came back "100% AI." Most humanizers are one- to ten-person shops that can only beat Pangram by making the text noticeably worse.

**False positives: 1 in 10,000, with an asterisk.** Pangram's headline false positive rate is about 1 in 10,000, closer to 1 in 5,000 at its 50-word minimum. Jacob does the math: across hundreds of assignments, some students will still be wrongly accused. Max makes two points in response. Pangram beats teachers' gut instinct, so it probably reduces false accusations overall, and a flag should lead to looking at drafts or Google Docs history, not an automatic verdict. The real gray zone is light or medium AI help, where Pangram says "100% AI" a few percent of the time, and Max says people tend to under-report their AI use ("I only used it for copy edits" can turn out to mean every word). The Taylor Lorenz Vanity Fair case was a true false positive: someone cherry-picked a 54-word passage, and the full article scored 100% human.

**Bias checks and the move into images.** Earlier detectors were accused of flagging non-native English speakers. Max says Pangram had 1 false positive in 25,000 ESL texts, an outside study found no bias against autistic writers, and a race analysis showed no significant difference. One trap he describes: humanizers add spelling mistakes, so a model trained carelessly on their output learns that errors mean AI, which unfairly hits ESL writers. The team threw out candidate models that showed that bias. The new image detector, released in late July, handles Gemini, GPT Image and Midjourney output and works on single video frames. Obvious customers include stock photo sites, Pinterest, dating apps, and real estate listings that quietly swap in AI "what it could look like" photos.

**Norms are still being written.** Both agree we're in a transition where some people let AI run their whole online presence and others swear never to touch it. Max expects some AI help to become normal, while replacing your own voice for a large audience stays frowned upon. Disclosure covers a lot of it. He also describes AI-heavy readers as a bell curve: newcomers can't spot AI, regular users can tell right away, and at the far end, people deep in "AI psychosis" read so much model output that they can't tell either.
fun_facts: The first AI-written thing Max found funny was an old GPT-2/3-era 4chan "greentext" about a bottomless pit supervisor whose pit stops being bottomless.
Max's recent favorite novel: Sublimation by Isabel J. Kim, about immigrants who split into two people, one who stays and one who leaves.
Jacob once called about a New York apartment and the landlord's first question was "How tall are you?" He passed.
Jacob says he was wrongly accused of plagiarism in high school, the old human version of a false positive.
discussion_questions: If labs like OpenAI may have commercial reasons not to make AI text detectable, should detection be done by independent companies like Pangram, by regulators (like the EU's watermark mandate), or both?
Max separates "compressing" (fine) from "padding" (a disservice). Would that test hold up as a disclosure rule for schools or newsrooms, and who decides which one you did?

highlights.text: Pangram sells AI-text detection mainly to schools and publishers. The goal is friction, not perfection: if you can't one-shot an assignment, fewer students bother cheating.
Publishing was blindsided by AI books because editors spend their days reading real books and never built an instinct for model prose.
Using AI to compress your own research into a shorter piece is fine. Using it to pad a few bullet points into an essay is a disservice to readers.
AI writing sounds the same because of mode collapse: models favour the most common phrasing, and post-training amplifies tics like "it's not just X, it's Y."
Watermarks are encoded statistically in word choice, so retyping won't remove them, but a paraphraser will. The EU now requires them on model text.
Pangram's false positive rate is about 1 in 10,000, but across hundreds of essays someone still gets flagged wrongly. A flag should prompt a look at drafts, not a verdict.
Training on humanizer output can teach a detector that spelling mistakes mean AI, which unfairly flags non-native English writers. Pangram discarded models that showed that bias.
AI image detection has obvious buyers: stock photo sites, Pinterest, dating apps and real estate listings that swap in AI "what it could look like" photos.

episodes.title: The playbook for building billion-dollar consumer brands
recap: **The 50 Cent deal: pay in equity, not cash.** In 2004 Vitaminwater was a great product nobody had heard of, with no budget for a star. Rohan got to 50 Cent through his manager Chris Lighty and pitched him directly: "I can't afford you, but I'll give you skin in the game." Fif agreed on the spot, adopted the brand as his own (he joked to the actual founder that he was the real founder of Vitaminwater), and made about 10x what Rohan had expected when Coca-Cola bought the company for $4.1B in 2007. That deal set the template for how celebrities and influencers get paid by brands.

**Influence the influencer, but only ones who actually like the product.** Rohan picked up "influence the influencer" on Sprite at Coke, working with Kobe Bryant, Missy Elliott and hip-hop culture, and used it to revive Powerade, which until then mostly got the athletes Gatorade passed on. His filter is that the talent has to genuinely like the brand, because then they go above and beyond. So he always insists on sitting down with the artist before signing: 50 for Vitaminwater, Justin Timberlake for Bai, Alix Earle for Poppi. For unknown founders, his advice is not to go around the agent. Build that relationship so they trust you, and make the sit-down the final step before the check, like a home inspection.

**Packaging is a brand you carry around.** Rohan's wife complains that a four-item grocery run takes him two hours because he studies every shelf. His view is that packaging can't come from research alone, since everyone uses the same agencies and gets the same ten designs. You need a clear idea of what the brand stands for, a strong creative team, and the willingness to trust your gut on the final pick.

**Before influencers, there were radio DJs.** In the pre-digital days, Rohan's version of influencer marketing was flying about 80 DJs from the top 60 US markets to Vegas around an awards show, so artists could hit 20 cities in an hour and a half. At Vitaminwater he hired field marketers who knew the DJs and the hot bartenders. The tactics change with each era, but the idea is the same: find who people already trust and get them excited first.

**CAVU: investors who help build the brand.** After the Coke exit, Rohan and hedge-fund partner Brett started CAVU ("Ceiling And Visibility Unlimited," a pilot's term for clear skies) to give founders a real edge on top of money. Rohan compares the firm to a Swiss Army knife: founders pick what they need, whether packaging, influencers, Amazon, DTC or billboards, while running their own show "80 to 90%." Good founders rarely walk in the door, so the team goes looking for them. His mantra is "brand is king," because without that moat there isn't much else.

**Poppi started by shutting the company down.** On Shark Tank, Rohan met a husband-and-wife team selling "Mother Beverage" in glass bottles. He hated the name and the packaging but loved the orange flavor (somewhere between Fanta and Orangina, with fiber and low sugar, what he calls "permissible"). His offer was to shut the company down and start a new one together. With CAVU funding it and Stevie handling the name and brand, they launched Poppi in March 2020. Two weeks later retailers dropped it because of COVID.

**COVID forced Poppi onto TikTok and Amazon.** With stores gone, Poppi went digital-first and Amazon-only. Allison Ellsworth's founder TikTok went viral, and an in-house team of young women who loved the brand built a community. The momentum grew until Hailey Bieber and Kylie Jenner were photographed drinking it without being paid. Then came Alix Earle on an equity deal, the 50 Cent model rebuilt for the creator era, which Rohan says "changed the game." Poppi later sold to Pepsi for close to $2B. His honest admission: "I was cool 20 years ago. I can see cool, but someone else has got to create the cool."

**The ones that got away.** Rohan's anti-portfolio includes The Ordinary, which they passed on because it would have taken a third of their first fund; it later sold for more than $2B and alone would have tripled the fund. The other is On running shoes. CAVU had a deal ready to sign, and that same day On announced Roger Federer, every existing investor re-upped, and CAVU was shut out of what would have been a 6–7x return. On whether a founder should be the face of the brand, he says it depends: Allison was for Poppi, but Madonna was a better face for Vita Coco than its founder.
fun_facts: Rohan is Indian by heritage, born and raised in Africa, educated in England, and now American.
He got fired from a manufacturing job at Mars (M&M's) before business school at Michigan.
At Coke, a mentor pitched him as "high risk, high reward. He's going to be brilliant or a train wreck."
CAVU's portfolio includes Once Upon a Farm, Noom and The Farmer's Dog.
Jeff Berman says he hasn't had a Coca-Cola in 17 years.
discussion_questions: Equity-for-influence worked for 50 Cent and Alix Earle when the brands were small. Does it still work now that every creator expects equity, or is the advantage gone once everyone does it?

Rohan's biggest misses (The Ordinary, On) came from being too cautious with fund concentration or too slow before a catalyst. How should a fund weigh a "too big a check" deal against the risk of missing a fund-making outcome?

highlights.text: Can't afford a star? Offer equity. 50 Cent took Vitaminwater stock instead of a fee and made about 10x what was expected when Coca-Cola paid $4.1B in 2007.
Only sign talent who genuinely like the product, and always sit down with them before the check. Treat it like a home inspection.
Packaging can't come from research alone: everyone uses the same agencies and gets the same ten designs. Know what the brand stands for and trust your gut on the final pick.
Before influencers there were radio DJs and bartenders. The tactic changes each era; the idea stays the same: find who people already trust and excite them first.
CAVU pitches itself as an investor that helps build the brand, from packaging to Amazon to billboards, because "brand is king" and is the only real moat in consumer goods.
Poppi began with Rohan telling the Shark Tank founders to shut their company down and relaunch with a new name and packaging. It later sold to Pepsi for close to $2B.
When COVID emptied stores two weeks after launch, Poppi went Amazon-only and built on the founder's viral TikTok and an in-house community team.
Rohan's anti-portfolio: passing on The Ordinary over fund concentration, which alone would have tripled the fund, and losing On the day it announced Roger Federer.
